bibl.title: Concurrent temporal channels for auditory processing: Oscillatory neural entrainment reveals segregation of function at different scales

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether the auditory system encodes temporal modulations equivalently across an intermediate range, or only within restricted bands
span.quote: Natural sounds convey perceptually relevant information over multiple timescales, and the necessary extraction of multi-timescale information requires the auditory system to work over distinct ranges. The simplest hypothesis suggests that temporal modulations are encoded in an equivalent manner within a reasonable intermediate range. We show that the human auditory system selectively and preferentially tracks acoustic dynamics concurrently at 2 timescales corresponding to the neurophysiological theta band (4–7 Hz) and gamma band ranges (31–45 Hz) but, contrary to expectation, not at the timescale corresponding to alpha (8–12 Hz), which has also been found to be related to auditory perception.

span.label: whether the alpha band, which a decade of studies ties to auditory perception, reflects the processing of acoustic information in the same way as the bands above and below it
span.quote: It is reasonable to hypothesize that the alpha band is fundamental to auditory perception, as demonstrated in a range of studies, but the timing (i.e., its intermediate position between lower theta and higher gamma activity) also invites the conjecture that alpha range activity reflects aspects of auditory processing on a timescale of approximately 100 ms. Here, we investigate directly the most straightforward hypothesis: does alpha band activity reflect the processing of acoustic information in a manner parallel to lower and higher neural frequencies?

span.label: two timescales track and the one between them does not - a hole in the middle of the range, which the paper reads as segregation of function in the time domain
span.quote: The results support the hypothesis that the human auditory system employs (at least) a 2-timescale processing mode, in which lower and higher perceptual sampling scales are segregated by an intermediate temporal regime in the alpha band that likely reflects different underlying computations.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: The results support the hypothesis that the human auditory system employs (at least) a 2-timescale processing mode, in which lower and higher perceptual sampling scales are segregated by an intermediate temporal regime in the alpha band that likely reflects different underlying computations.

span.label: oscillatory neural entrainment to acoustic timescales
span.quote: In this MEG-based neurophysiological experiment, we investigate temporal coding at different scales by exploring the entrainment of auditory cortical oscillations to sounds with different modulation rates.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: Listeners heard synthetic acoustic stimuli with temporally modulated structures at 3 timescales (approximately 190-, approximately 100-, and approximately 30-ms modulation periods) and identified the stimuli while undergoing magnetoencephalography recording.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: theta oscillations both track slow acoustic dynamics and actively chunk faster-modulated sounds into theta-period units, which is why theta phase carries information about every modulation rate
span.quote: One possible explanation is that theta band oscillations (i) track acoustic dynamics at that specific temporal scale and (ii) at the same time actively chunk (at a scale of the mean theta band period) sounds with faster modulation rates, so that acoustic properties over larger scales can be further extracted [ 85 ].

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: alpha activity suppresses task-irrelevant cortical areas and thereby sits between, and segregates, the theta and gamma coding regimes as a top-down modulator instead of coding acoustic timing itself
span.quote: The alpha band is associated with suppressing activity of cortical areas that are irrelevant for ongoing sensory processing according to tasks [ 87 ], which suggests (for the current context) that alpha band oscillations co-occur with and segregate 2 temporal coding regimes (theta and gamma bands) and modulate auditory processing as a top-down process [ 88 ].

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: beta-band phase is random with respect to the stimulus, so it injects noise into the decoder and dropping it improves classification
span.quote: The random phase in the beta band adds more noise to the classification process, so removing the phase information of the beta band actually results in better classification performance.

span.label: the theta band does two jobs - it tracks acoustic dynamics at its own scale AND chunks faster sounds into units about 200 ms long, which is why it decodes stimuli of every rate
span.quote: phase series in the theta band temporally track acoustic dynamics across all modulation rates (used in our study), which suggests that the theta band is not only entrained by modulation rates with corresponding frequency range but also chunks sounds with modulation rates outside of the theta band range into acoustic segments at a timescale corresponding to the theta period range. The gamma band specifically locks to modulation rates with a timescale corresponding to gamma band, approximately 30 ms. The contribution of the alpha band must be seen as functionally separate from the other bands.

span.label: while the gamma band locks specifically to the corresponding rate, about 30 ms, and contributes only to classifying those sounds
span.quote: phase series in the theta band temporally track acoustic dynamics across all modulation rates (used in our study), which suggests that the theta band is not only entrained by modulation rates with corresponding frequency range but also chunks sounds with modulation rates outside of the theta band range into acoustic segments at a timescale corresponding to the theta period range. The gamma band specifically locks to modulation rates with a timescale corresponding to gamma band, approximately 30 ms. The contribution of the alpha band must be seen as functionally separate from the other bands.

span.label: and the alpha band, rather than tracking, co-occurs with and segregates the two coding regimes as a top-down process - attention, working memory, listening effort, functional inhibition
span.quote: The absence or marked reduction of tracking acoustic dynamics in the alpha band suggests that neural activity reflected in the alpha band may play a different role in audition. In the auditory system, the neural computations reflected in the alpha band signal may be more explicitly involved in auditory attention, working memory, listening effort, or functional inhibition [ 34 , 36 – 39 , 86 ], and the alpha band may as such be more related to aspects of auditory perception that differ from constructing the elementary perceptual representations.

span.label: so continuous sound is chunked by temporal windows of two different sizes, one centered around 200 ms and the other around 30 ms
span.quote: As natural sounds contain information at multiple scales, the auditory system may chunk continuous sounds using temporal windows of different sizes to sample information at different timescales, instead of processing acoustic information on a unitary scale. This multiplexing strategy solves the requirement in auditory processing that both fine resolution and integration over time are needed for perceiving sounds with regularities both at large and small scales. One model proposes that, although a very high resolution is represented in subcortical areas, in the auditory cortex, there are 2 main temporal windows used for processing acoustic information: one centered around 200 ms and the other around 30 ms

span.label: The behavioral identification task may be confounded by selection bias, because theta and gamma sounds sit at the perceptual extremes of the stimulus set.
span.quote: However, the behavioral method used in the present study cannot circumvent a concern with a selection bias to different sounds, because participants may identify θ sounds and γ sounds more easily simply because the modulation rates of these 2 sounds are located at the perceptual extremes in this experimental design.

span.label: The behavioral task was suboptimal and served mainly to maintain attention, so the behavioral data are not interpreted strongly.
span.quote: We acknowledge that this behavioral task is suboptimal—and primarily employed to ensure attention during neurophysiological recording—so we scrupulously refrain from overinterpreting these data, beyond pointing out that the pattern is consistent with our hypothesis.

span.label: Mutual information estimates are biased by the finite number of trials and required a quadratic extrapolation correction.
span.quote: The estimation of mutual information is subject to bias caused by finite sampling of the probability distributions because limited data were supplied in the present study (a finite number of trials).

span.label: A SELECTION BIAS ADMITTED WITH SELF-RESTRAINT AS THE REMEDY: participants may identify the theta and gamma sounds more easily simply because those rates sit AT THE PERCEPTUAL EXTREMES of the design - the task is called SUBOPTIMAL and the authors SCRUPULOUSLY REFRAIN FROM OVERINTERPRETING the data
span.quote: However, the behavioral method used in the present study cannot circumvent a concern with a selection bias to different sounds, because participants may identify θ sounds and γ sounds more easily simply because the modulation rates of these 2 sounds are located at the perceptual extremes in this experimental design. We acknowledge that this behavioral task is suboptimal—and primarily employed to ensure attention during neurophysiological recording—so we scrupulously refrain from overinterpreting these data, beyond pointing out that the pattern is consistent with our hypothesis.

span.label: the gamma band contribution to decoding is not significant with all subjects and is significant AFTER REMOVING 1 SUBJECT who showed abnormal decoding performance - both numbers printed
span.quote: Before adjusted FDR correction, the gamma band shows a contribution to decoding γ sounds ( t (14) = 2.07, p = 0.057, d = 0.53). After removing 1 subject who showed abnormal decoding performance, we found that the gamma band significantly contributes to decoding γ sounds after FDR correction

span.label: and a real gamma effect comes out non-significant because the band is defined 30 to 45 Hz while the coherence PEAKS WITHIN A NARROW RANGE CENTERED AROUND 37 Hz - averaging over the band decreases the mean
span.quote: zITC of γ sounds in the gamma band is not significant ( t (14) = −0.15, p = 1.00, d = −0.03), likely because robust phase coherence peaks within a narrow frequency range centered around 37 Hz, as shown in the spectrum of zITC in Fig 1a . Averaging zITC of γ sound from 30 to 45 Hz decreases the mean of zITC in the gamma band.

span.label: with one participant excluded for recording noise before any analysis, leaving 15
span.quote: We excluded the data from 1 participant because of noise issues during neurophysiological recording. Therefore, the analysis included the data from 15 participants (8 females; mean age: 25.2; standard deviation: 3.0).

span.label: the band names theta, alpha and gamma, applied to the STIMULUS as well as to the brain - the stimulus type with a modulation rate in theta band range is called a theta sound
span.quote: We refer to the stimulus type with a modulation rate in theta band range (4–7 Hz) as a theta (θ) sound, the stimulus type with modulation rate in the alpha band range (8–12 Hz) as an alpha ( α ) sound, and the stimulus type with modulation rate in the gamma band range (30–45 Hz) as a gamma (γ) sound.

span.label: mutual information between the phase series and the acoustic structure, used to separate tracking from mere entrainment
span.quote: The results of the mutual information analyses demonstrate that phase patterns in the theta and gamma bands track the temporal structure of the stimuli, as quantified by the cochlear-scaled correlation. The robust phase coherence observed in the theta band for θ sounds and that in the gamma band for γ sounds is indeed caused by tracking specific acoustic structures, rather than simply being evoked by generic acoustic stimuli.

span.label: cochlear-scaled entropy, turned into an index called cochlear-scaled correlation that marks the acoustic edges of the stimulus
span.quote: To quantify the acoustic edges and extract the temporal structure of the stimuli, inspired by the concept of cochlear-scaled entropy [ 112 ], we created an index, cochlear-scaled correlation. We first used a Gammatone filterbank of 64 banks, ranging from 50 Hz to 22,050 Hz, to decompose the sounds and extracted the envelope of each cochlear band. Then, a moving average window of 10 ms was applied on the envelope of each cochlear band to create a vector of length 64 at each time point. We computed the Pearson’s correlation between 2 vectors of adjacent time points and the correlation results were then down-sampled to a sampling rate of 100 Hz, which corresponds to the sampling rate of the phase series of the MEG signals. The cochlear-scaled correlation for each sound is shown in Fig 4a . The visualization shows that cochlear-scaled correlation can confer the temporal structure of stimuli. Within a frequency sweep segment, the cochlear-scaled correlation is high—close to 1—and at the boundaries of frequency sweep segments, a sudden drop of correlation coefficient is evident. The temporal structure of these sudden drops of correlation efficiency correlates with modulation rates, with the θ sound having the fewest drops and the γ sound having the most drops.

span.label: segregation of function, carried from the spatial domain into the time domain
span.quote: This design, however, builds in a hole in processing, a segregation of function between low and high processing rates—perhaps optimized for sensory sampling—by an intermediate rate, perhaps optimized for allocating attentional and memory resources and functionally inhibiting task- or stimulus-irrelevant actions. Whereas we typically address segregation of function in the spatial domain, i.e., different regions are specialized for different operations, here, we provide a compelling example of cortical segregation of function in the time domain.

span.label: the onset time of each trial randomized and the whole ITC analysis re-run 1,000 times to build a null distribution
span.quote: As the baselines of phase-locking may be different across frequency bands, which may be affected by power distributions with a 1/f characteristic, a shuffling method of onset time was used to avoid this confound. Within each condition, the onset time of the stimulus was randomly chosen on each trial and a new dataset for each condition was created. The same analysis of ITC was applied on this new dataset. To create a distribution of shuffled ITCs, this shuffling procedure was repeated 1,000 times.

span.label: mutual information computed against the phase series evoked by the OTHER two sounds
span.quote: For example, when we computed MI between the cochlear-scaled correlation of the θ sounds and the 3 phase series evoked, respectively, by θ , α , and γ sounds, we used the phase series evoked by α and γ sounds as control conditions and examined whether MI between the cochlear-scaled correlation of θ sounds and the phase series evoked by θ sounds is significant.

span.label: quadratic extrapolation over subsets of trials, taking the zero-crossing as the estimate
span.quote: The estimation of mutual information is subject to bias caused by finite sampling of the probability distributions because limited data were supplied in the present study (a finite number of trials). Therefore, a quadratic extrapolation embedded in the Information Breakdown Toolbox was applied to correct bias. MI is computed on various subsets of the trials of the dataset of each condition. A quadratic function is then fit to these data points, and the actual mutual information is taken to be the zero-crossing value. This new value reflects the estimated mutual information for an infinite number of trials and greatly reduces the finite sampling bias

span.label: classification run on power as well as on phase
span.quote: A Stimulus-type × Classification source (phase classification or power classification) 2-way rmANOVA reveals the main effect of Classification source ( F (1,14) = 30.44, p < 0.001, η p 2 = 0.685), with the D′ of phase-based classification significantly larger than the D′ of power-based classification. To determine whether classification performance is better than chance (D′ = 0), a 1-sample t test with Bonferroni correction was applied on each stimulus type and each classification source. For phase classification, the performance of all stimulus types was better than chance (for θ sounds, t (14) = 6.19, p < 0.001, d = 1.60; for α sounds, t (14) = 6.40, p < 0.001, d = 1.65; for γ sounds, t (14) = 6.44, p < 0.001, d = 1.66). For power classification, classification performance of α sounds was significant ( t (14) = 4.73, p = 0.002, d = 1.22) as well as θ sounds ( t (14) = 3.10, p = 0.046, d = 0.80), but performance of power classification was only slightly above chance. These results demonstrate that phase patterns of cortical oscillations reliably encode the temporal dynamics of stimuli.

span.label: the multiple-comparison policy fixed by the number of comparisons rather than chosen per test
span.quote: When multiple comparisons were performed, to control familywise error rate and, at the same time, not to cause a high rate of false negatives, the Bonferroni correction was used when there were less than 10 comparisons performed, and an adjusted FDR was used when there were more than 10 comparisons performed

span.label: THE SIMPLEST HYPOTHESIS, STATED IN ORDER TO BE FALSIFIED: temporal modulations are encoded IN AN EQUIVALENT MANNER within a reasonable intermediate range - and the finding is that the system tracks at theta and gamma BUT, CONTRARY TO EXPECTATION, NOT AT ALPHA
span.quote: Natural sounds convey perceptually relevant information over multiple timescales, and the necessary extraction of multi-timescale information requires the auditory system to work over distinct ranges. The simplest hypothesis suggests that temporal modulations are encoded in an equivalent manner within a reasonable intermediate range. We show that the human auditory system selectively and preferentially tracks acoustic dynamics concurrently at 2 timescales corresponding to the neurophysiological theta band (4–7 Hz) and gamma band ranges (31–45 Hz) but, contrary to expectation, not at the timescale corresponding to alpha (8–12 Hz), which has also been found to be related to auditory perception.

span.label: THE HEADLINE IS A NEGATIVE RESULT: CRUCIALLY, NO ROBUST PHASE COHERENCE WAS FOUND IN THE ALPHA AND BETA BANDS - and this nonuniform pattern DOES NOT SUPPORT the simplest hypothesis of comparable neural tracking for all rates
span.quote: Crucially, no robust phase coherence was found in the alpha and beta bands. This nonuniform phase-response pattern across temporal regimes does not support the simplest hypothesis of comparable neural tracking for all stimulus modulation rates.

span.label: and the null is about the band the field had every reason to expect: IT IS REASONABLE TO HYPOTHESIZE THAT THE ALPHA BAND IS FUNDAMENTAL TO AUDITORY PERCEPTION, AS DEMONSTRATED IN A RANGE OF STUDIES - attention, working memory, listening effort, speech intelligibility
span.quote: It is reasonable to hypothesize that the alpha band is fundamental to auditory perception, as demonstrated in a range of studies, but the timing (i.e., its intermediate position between lower theta and higher gamma activity) also invites the conjecture that alpha range activity reflects aspects of auditory processing on a timescale of approximately 100 ms. Here, we investigate directly the most straightforward hypothesis: does alpha band activity reflect the processing of acoustic information in a manner parallel to lower and higher neural frequencies?

span.label: with the same null reached by a second, independent measure: NO SIGNIFICANT MAIN EFFECTS of the phase sound type were found for mutual information computed using the cochlear-scaled correlation of alpha sounds
span.quote: Importantly, no significant main effects of the phase sound type were found for mutual information computed using the cochlear-scaled correlation of α sounds.

span.label: and a third: the alpha band DID NOT CONTRIBUTE SIGNIFICANTLY TO DECODING ANY STIMULI, while the beta band DETERIORATED decoding of gamma sounds
span.quote: The beta band deteriorated decoding of γ sounds ( t (14) = −4.66, p = 0.002, d = 1.20). Crucially, the alpha band did not contribute significantly to decoding any stimuli.

span.label: A BAND WIDER THAN THE EFFECT IT IS MEANT TO MEASURE: the gamma coherence is real but comes out NOT SIGNIFICANT because it PEAKS WITHIN A NARROW FREQUENCY RANGE CENTERED AROUND 37 Hz, and AVERAGING FROM 30 TO 45 Hz DECREASES THE MEAN - the analysis window, not the brain, decides the verdict
span.quote: zITC of γ sounds in the gamma band is not significant ( t (14) = −0.15, p = 1.00, d = −0.03), likely because robust phase coherence peaks within a narrow frequency range centered around 37 Hz, as shown in the spectrum of zITC in Fig 1a . Averaging zITC of γ sound from 30 to 45 Hz decreases the mean of zITC in the gamma band.

span.label: A CLAIM THAT IS NULL AND SIGNIFICANT DEPENDING ON ONE EXCLUSION, WITH BOTH NUMBERS PRINTED: before correction the gamma band shows a contribution at p = 0.057, and AFTER REMOVING 1 SUBJECT who showed abnormal decoding performance it is significant after FDR correction
span.quote: Before adjusted FDR correction, the gamma band shows a contribution to decoding γ sounds ( t (14) = 2.07, p = 0.057, d = 0.53). After removing 1 subject who showed abnormal decoding performance, we found that the gamma band significantly contributes to decoding γ sounds after FDR correction

span.label: THE DISAMBIGUATION LIVES IN THE TYPOGRAPHY: in one sentence the Greek letter names the STIMULUS and the spelled-out word names the SIGNIFICANCE LEVEL - the alpha and gamma sounds evoked coherence above 1.64, THE CRITICAL Z-SCORE EQUIVALENT TO AN ALPHA LEVEL OF 0.05. Alphabet, not wording, carries the distinction, and alphabet is the first thing text extraction destroys
span.quote: However, the α and γ sounds also evoked robust phase coherence at a frequency range below 8 Hz, in which zITC of the group means for α and γ sounds are above 1.64—the critical z -score equivalent to an alpha level of 0.05 (1-tailed, Bonferroni corrected).

span.label: AND THE STIMULUS IS NAMED AFTER THE BRAIN: we refer to the stimulus type with a modulation rate in theta band range AS A THETA SOUND, and likewise for alpha and gamma - so every result sentence carries the same word for the sound and for the neural band that may or may not track it
span.quote: We refer to the stimulus type with a modulation rate in theta band range (4–7 Hz) as a theta (θ) sound, the stimulus type with modulation rate in the alpha band range (8–12 Hz) as an alpha ( α ) sound, and the stimulus type with modulation rate in the gamma band range (30–45 Hz) as a gamma (γ) sound.

span.label: with the band edges moving between sections: the stimuli were aligned to theta (4-7 Hz), ALPHA/LOW BETA (8-15 Hz) and low gamma (30-45 Hz), while the analysis bands are alpha (8-12 Hz) and gamma (31-45 Hz) - the alpha sound's own range is written twice with different edges
span.quote: The distribution of the segment durations of the stimuli aligned with the range of periods typical of theta (4–7 Hz), alpha/low beta (8–15 Hz), and low gamma (30–45 Hz) band neural oscillations. We refer to the stimulus type with mean segment duration of 190 ms as a theta ( θ ) sound, the stimulus type with mean segment duration of 100 ms as an alpha ( α ) sound, and the stimulus type with mean segment duration of 27 ms as a gamma ( γ ) sound.

span.label: and the analysis bands stated exactly, which is what makes the mismatch visible at all: theta (4-7 Hz), alpha (8-12 Hz), beta (13-30 Hz), and gamma (31-45 Hz)
span.quote: The ITC and power data were averaged from 0.3 s to 1.8 s poststimulus onset to minimize the effects of stimulus-evoked onsets and offsets and within 4 frequency bands: theta (4–7 Hz), alpha (8–12 Hz), beta (13–30 Hz), and gamma (31–45 Hz).

span.label: ENTRAINMENT IS NOT TRACKING, AND THE PAPER SAYS SO BEFORE MEASURING ANYTHING: cortical oscillations entrained by stimuli of corresponding frequencies ARE NOT SUFFICIENT to demonstrate the importance of a band, because the entrainment could simply reflect A MODULATION-FREQUENCY FOLLOWING RESPONSE WHICH MAY HAVE LITTLE TO DO WITH the system actively processing acoustic information
span.quote: Although these findings demonstrate dominant auditory responses in the low frequency range (delta-theta and alpha) and the gamma band, the cortical oscillations entrained by stimuli of corresponding frequencies of the regular modulation are not sufficient to demonstrate the importance of theta, alpha, and gamma bands in auditory processing, because the entrainment could simply reflect a modulation-frequency following response which may have little to do with the auditory system actively processing acoustic information in the theta and gamma bands.

span.label: which is exactly what the mutual information analysis is for - the coherence is INDEED CAUSED BY TRACKING SPECIFIC ACOUSTIC STRUCTURES, RATHER THAN SIMPLY BEING EVOKED BY GENERIC ACOUSTIC STIMULI
span.quote: The results of the mutual information analyses demonstrate that phase patterns in the theta and gamma bands track the temporal structure of the stimuli, as quantified by the cochlear-scaled correlation. The robust phase coherence observed in the theta band for θ sounds and that in the gamma band for γ sounds is indeed caused by tracking specific acoustic structures, rather than simply being evoked by generic acoustic stimuli.

span.label: and the one place the two come apart: gamma sounds evoke robust coherence IN THE THETA BAND with NO specialized tracking there, which is read as the theta band CHUNKING rather than coding - a perceptual unit on a timescale of approximately 200 ms
span.quote: We did not find specialized tracking for γ sounds in the theta band, although γ sounds evoked robust phase coherence in the theta band ( Fig 2a ). This could be because the theta band, instead of faithfully coding the temporal structure of γ sounds, chunks acoustic information and forms a perceptual unit on a timescale of approximately 200 ms (the theta band range).

span.label: A SELECTION BIAS ADMITTED, WITH SELF-RESTRAINT AS THE REMEDY: participants may identify theta and gamma sounds more easily simply because those rates ARE LOCATED AT THE PERCEPTUAL EXTREMES in this design - the task is SUBOPTIMAL, and WE SCRUPULOUSLY REFRAIN FROM OVERINTERPRETING THESE DATA
span.quote: However, the behavioral method used in the present study cannot circumvent a concern with a selection bias to different sounds, because participants may identify θ sounds and γ sounds more easily simply because the modulation rates of these 2 sounds are located at the perceptual extremes in this experimental design. We acknowledge that this behavioral task is suboptimal—and primarily employed to ensure attention during neurophysiological recording—so we scrupulously refrain from overinterpreting these data, beyond pointing out that the pattern is consistent with our hypothesis.

span.label: THE MEASURE'S MAGNITUDE IS NOT ITS INFORMATION: temporal coding capability DOES NOT CORRESPOND TO THE MAGNITUDE OF THE MTF - LARGE ITC VALUES FOR THE ALPHA BAND DO NOT INDICATE HIGH TEMPORAL CODING CAPABILITY
span.quote: The classification results also reveal data patterns that have not been shown in previous findings on the MTF. As the MTF shows decreased neural responses with increasing modulation rate, it is plausible to conjecture that temporal coding for acoustic dynamics would also show such a pattern. However, as observed in the classification analysis, the temporal coding capability does not correspond to the magnitude of the MTF—large ITC values for the alpha band do not indicate high temporal coding capability.

span.label: and phase carries what power does not - phase-based classification is significantly better than power-based, which was only slightly above chance
span.quote: A Stimulus-type × Classification source (phase classification or power classification) 2-way rmANOVA reveals the main effect of Classification source ( F (1,14) = 30.44, p < 0.001, η p 2 = 0.685), with the D′ of phase-based classification significantly larger than the D′ of power-based classification. To determine whether classification performance is better than chance (D′ = 0), a 1-sample t test with Bonferroni correction was applied on each stimulus type and each classification source. For phase classification, the performance of all stimulus types was better than chance (for θ sounds, t (14) = 6.19, p < 0.001, d = 1.60; for α sounds, t (14) = 6.40, p < 0.001, d = 1.65; for γ sounds, t (14) = 6.44, p < 0.001, d = 1.66). For power classification, classification performance of α sounds was significant ( t (14) = 4.73, p = 0.002, d = 1.22) as well as θ sounds ( t (14) = 3.10, p = 0.046, d = 0.80), but performance of power classification was only slightly above chance. These results demonstrate that phase patterns of cortical oscillations reliably encode the temporal dynamics of stimuli.

span.label: A CONCEPT MOVED FROM SPACE TO TIME: whereas we typically address segregation of function IN THE SPATIAL DOMAIN, different regions specialised for different operations, HERE WE PROVIDE A COMPELLING EXAMPLE OF CORTICAL SEGREGATION OF FUNCTION IN THE TIME DOMAIN
span.quote: This design, however, builds in a hole in processing, a segregation of function between low and high processing rates—perhaps optimized for sensory sampling—by an intermediate rate, perhaps optimized for allocating attentional and memory resources and functionally inhibiting task- or stimulus-irrelevant actions. Whereas we typically address segregation of function in the spatial domain, i.e., different regions are specialized for different operations, here, we provide a compelling example of cortical segregation of function in the time domain.

span.label: with the negative space named as design rather than as absence - this design BUILDS IN A HOLE IN PROCESSING, a segregation between low and high rates BY AN INTERMEDIATE RATE
span.quote: This design, however, builds in a hole in processing, a segregation of function between low and high processing rates—perhaps optimized for sensory sampling—by an intermediate rate, perhaps optimized for allocating attentional and memory resources and functionally inhibiting task- or stimulus-irrelevant actions. Whereas we typically address segregation of function in the spatial domain, i.e., different regions are specialized for different operations, here, we provide a compelling example of cortical segregation of function in the time domain.

span.label: and the result is claimed as general because the stimuli were not speech: based on NONSPEECH stimuli, such dual-scale entrainment IS NOT SPEECH SPECIFIC but may rather reflect AN INTRINSIC AUDITORY PROCESSING PROPERTY
span.quote: Importantly, our results, based on nonspeech stimuli, suggest that such dual-scale entrainment is not speech specific but may rather reflect an intrinsic auditory processing property. The auditory cortex tunes to both theta frequency and gamma frequency acoustic dynamics [ 65 ]. The alpha band reflects different operations.

span.label: a strictly hierarchical model ruled out in the introduction - short windows concatenated into longer ones CANNOT BY ITSELF MEET THE PERCEPTUAL DEMANDS
span.quote: A strictly hierarchical model, starting, say, with short/small integration windows at more peripheral processing regions, which are then concatenated to build longer windows, cannot by itself meet the perceptual demands

span.label: and the behavioral asymmetry that motivates everything: all clean stimuli identified well, with REDUCED PERFORMANCE IN CORRECTLY IDENTIFYING THE ALPHA SOUNDS ACROSS ALL LEVELS compared to both gamma and theta
span.quote: The results ( Fig 1b ) demonstrate that participants identified all clean stimuli well (all d′ > 2) and that performance deteriorated in all conditions as the SNR level decreased. Particularly noteworthy is the reduced performance in correctly identifying the α sounds across all levels compared to both γ and θ sounds.

span.label: builds-on → Boemio et al. (2005) and Luo and Poeppel (2012)
span.quote: Building on experiments by Boemio et al. (2005) [ 65 ] and Luo and Poeppel (2012) [ 66 ], we generated acoustic stimuli with modulation rates that were centered at the typical periods of the neural theta (4–7 Hz), alpha-beta (8–15 Hz), and gamma (31–45 Hz) frequency bands

span.label: replicates → previous electrophysiological data of monkey primary auditory cortex (reference 73)
span.quote: Importantly, the failure to observe entrainment in the alpha and beta bands in the present study also aligns with previous electrophysiological data of monkey primary auditory cortex: cortical oscillations could entrain to modulation rates in the delta-theta bands but not at 12 Hz [ 73 ].

span.label: replicates → a recent psychophysical study of concurrent short and long timescale auditory processing (reference 95)
span.quote: Notwithstanding this potential concern, results from a recent psychophysical study dovetail with the view that the auditory system works concurrently on a short timescale (about 30 ms) to extract fine-grained acoustic temporal detail while processing more global acoustic patterns on a longer timescale (>200 ms) [ 95 ].

span.label: contradicts → the simplest hypothesis, that temporal modulations are encoded equivalently across an intermediate range
span.quote: Natural sounds convey perceptually relevant information over multiple timescales, and the necessary extraction of multi-timescale information requires the auditory system to work over distinct ranges. The simplest hypothesis suggests that temporal modulations are encoded in an equivalent manner within a reasonable intermediate range. We show that the human auditory system selectively and preferentially tracks acoustic dynamics concurrently at 2 timescales corresponding to the neurophysiological theta band (4–7 Hz) and gamma band ranges (31–45 Hz) but, contrary to expectation, not at the timescale corresponding to alpha (8–12 Hz), which has also been found to be related to auditory perception.

span.label: critiques → entrainment to regular modulations as evidence that a band actively processes acoustic information
span.quote: Although these findings demonstrate dominant auditory responses in the low frequency range (delta-theta and alpha) and the gamma band, the cortical oscillations entrained by stimuli of corresponding frequencies of the regular modulation are not sufficient to demonstrate the importance of theta, alpha, and gamma bands in auditory processing, because the entrainment could simply reflect a modulation-frequency following response which may have little to do with the auditory system actively processing acoustic information in the theta and gamma bands.

span.label: contradicts → the expectation from the modulation transfer function that temporal coding capability follows response magnitude
span.quote: The classification results also reveal data patterns that have not been shown in previous findings on the MTF. As the MTF shows decreased neural responses with increasing modulation rate, it is plausible to conjecture that temporal coding for acoustic dynamics would also show such a pattern. However, as observed in the classification analysis, the temporal coding capability does not correspond to the magnitude of the MTF—large ITC values for the alpha band do not indicate high temporal coding capability.
